extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journalists, and readers interested in retractions and research integrity
extracted.subtask_description: A journalistic-blog discussion of scientific paper retractions, the reasons they occur, the editorial responses (erratum, expression of concern, retraction), and the role of investigative reporting and peer review in detecting problems. Focused on high-profile misconduct cases and their impacts on fields and journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectrum of corrections: erratum → expression of concern → retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: A glossary of the spectrum between erratum and retraction — including expression of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes minor technical slips (erratum) from more serious problems that may require pulling the entire article (retraction). Editors may also issue an 'expression of concern' as an intermediate notice when validity is questioned. Example: The Lancet Oncology issued an 'expression of concern' about a 2007 paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for retraction (causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions are born of many mothers. Fraud is the most titillating reason, and mercifully the most rare, but when it happens the results can be devastating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes fabricated data, invented statistical analyses, falsification, and other forms of misconduct or serious error. Examples cited: Anil Potti (invented key statistical analyses), Scott Reuben (fabrications led to more than a score of retractions), and Andrew Wakefield (work called a 'hoax' by the BMJ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of peer review and editorial vetting as quality filters
rubrics_metrics.description: Science journals have the luxury of time. Thorough vetting, through editorial boards, peer reviewers and other filters, is the coin of the realm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review and editorial oversight are the primary formal mechanisms to prevent errors and misconduct, but they are not infallible — mistakes and misconduct can still slip through, sometimes requiring expressions of concern or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of investigative journalism in uncovering misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic investigation can reveal the true details of problematic research and prompt editorial action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece highlights Brian Deer’s investigation (which exposed issues in Wakefield's work) and notes that such reporting can lead journals or the public to re-evaluate published findings. The BMJ's call that Wakefield’s work was a 'hoax' is an example of journalism prompting scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of retractions on disciplines and trust
rubrics_metrics.description: When fraud or major errors occur, the consequences can be severe, affecting an entire medical specialty or field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Scott Reuben’s case, where fabrications led to the retraction of many papers and deeply rattled an entire specialty — implying that severity/scale is a relevant evaluative dimension when assessing misconduct and appropriate corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial use of 'expression of concern' as an interim step
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may issue an 'expression of concern' about the validity of a paper when serious questions arise but before a full retraction is decided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a public flag that the paper’s findings are under question; described in the text with the Lancet Oncology example and characterized colloquially as a Britishism akin to 'Holy Shit!' pending further investigation.
